summary.title: Build vs. Buy
summary.one_liner: A simple rule for deciding whether to build a component yourself or buy one: build only when it is high cost, tightly integrated, and difficult to design; buy everything else.
keywords: when to build your own software
takeaways: Build a component only if it is high cost, tightly integrated with the system, and difficult to design; otherwise buy it, including open source options.
Becoming an expert requires designing, running, and maintaining a component, so organisations have limited capacity for expertise and should spend it on competitive advantages.
Skunk Works built only what satisfied the main selling point and its primary challenge, using off-the-shelf parts for everything else.
Simple subsets of third-party tools may be worth building yourself, but beware of Greenspun's tenth rule, where you reimplement complicated features anyway.
summary.summary: The author presents a short heuristic for the build-versus-buy decision: build a component only if it is high cost, tightly integrated, and difficult to design, and buy everything else. The reasoning is that evaluating or safely buying a critical component requires deep expertise, which an organisation has limited capacity for, so expertise should go to competitive advantages. The post illustrates this with Lockheed Skunk Works, which custom-built the parts behind the F-117's main selling point and the SR-71's speed-related heat problems while using off-the-shelf parts elsewhere. It closes with a caveat about simplicity and Greenspun's tenth rule, using a Kubernetes reimplementation anecdote.
